instantiated_cells.justification: The definition of “lobbyist” turns on being paid for, or having principal duties of, “communicat[ing] directly” to influence legislative/administrative action, and “payment to influence” includes payments for direct communication or urging others to communicate, but the statute does not enumerate specific communication modes (oral, written, emails, etc.).

California defines a lobbyist as an individual paid to communicate to influence legislative/administrative action (covering both contract/professional and employee/in-house lobbyists), requires lobbying firms and lobbyist employers to register or report, and covers “person[s]” broadly (including organizations and agencies) while exempting elected officials/state employees acting in official capacity.

Coverage is triggered by objective thresholds (e.g., $2,000/month compensation for an individual lobbyist and $5,000/quarter payments to influence), not by a discretionary materiality test allowing exemption.

A lobbyist is defined by communications with elective state officials and legislative officials to influence legislative action, and “legislative action” expressly includes the Governor’s approval or veto of bills.

The statute covers influencing both “legislative action” and “administrative action,” meaning lobbying targets include the Legislature/Governor as well as state agencies involved in rulemaking and quasi-legislative proceedings.
The lobbyist definition includes communicating with legislative officials/elective state officials to influence legislative action, which includes the Governor’s bill approval or veto.
Lobbying is defined to include communications with legislative officials and elective state officials to influence legislative action, which is defined to include action by the Governor.

Because “legislative action” includes Governor approval/veto and lobbyists are those paid to communicate with elective state officials/legislative officials to influence such action, the definition includes both legislative and executive officials.
Lobbying covers influencing “administrative action,” defined as state agency rulemaking and quasi-legislative proceedings, thus reaching the administrative/bureaucratic branch as lobbying targets.
Elected public officials acting in their official capacity (and state employees acting within scope of employment) are exempt from Chapter 6’s lobbying provisions rather than required to register.

While state employees acting within scope are exempt, the law contemplates public employees who would otherwise meet the lobbyist compensation/principal-duties communication standard, imposing at least the $10/month gift limit on those non-legislative employees attempting to influence legislative action.

The operative lobbying definitions apply to any “person” or business entity meeting compensation/communication criteria and do not rely on public charter or special governmental protections as definitional elements.

A “lobbying firm” is defined in part by whether any partner, owner, officer, or employee is a lobbyist, and registration requires listing those partners/owners/officers/employees, tying the definition to ownership/partner status.

The definitions of lobbyist, lobbying firm, and lobbyist employer are based on compensation and activities (and, for firms, having a lobbyist partner/employee), not on revenue composition or structural funding sources.
